questions.stem: If $4$ times a number is increased by $6$, the result is $15$ less than the square of the number. Mark on the number line every number that fits this story.

canonical_solution.text_md: Let the number be $n$. "4 times the number, increased by 6" is $4n + 6$, and "15 less than the square of the number" is $n^2 - 15$.
The story says these are equal: $4n + 6 = n^2 - 15$.
Bring every term to one side, so the equation equals zero: $n^2 - 4n - 21 = 0$.
Factorise, and test the middle term by multiplying out: $(n - 7)(n + 3) = 0$ gives $-7n + 3n = -4n$ and $-7 \times 3 = -21$.
A product is zero only when a factor is zero, so $n - 7 = 0$ or $n + 3 = 0$: $n = 7$ or $n = -3$.

Check each solution against the story. The problem puts no condition on the sign of the number. $n = 7$: $4(7) + 6 = 34$ and $7^2 - 15 = 34$. $n = -3$: $4(-3) + 6 = -6$ and $(-3)^2 - 15 = -6$. Both fit, so both are kept.
Mark $-3$ and $7$ on the number line.

questions.stem: The length of a rectangle is twice its breadth, and its area is $128\ \text{cm}^2$. Let the breadth be $b$ cm. Mark on the number line every value of $b$ that is possible for this rectangle.

canonical_solution.text_md: Let the breadth be $b$ cm, so the length is $2b$ cm.
Area = length $\times$ breadth, so $2b \times b = 128$, which is $2b^2 = 128$.
Bring every term to one side and divide both sides by $2$: $b^2 - 64 = 0$.
Factorise as a difference of squares: $(b - 8)(b + 8) = 0$.
A product is zero only when a factor is zero, so $b = 8$ or $b = -8$.

Check each solution against the story. The breadth is a length, and a length cannot be negative, so $b = -8$ is ruled out. $b = 8$ gives a length of $16$ cm and an area of $8 \times 16 = 128\ \text{cm}^2$, which fits.
Mark only $8$ on the number line.

questions.stem: In the formula $I=\dfrac{bh^2}{12}$, $b=18$ and $I=54$. Mark on the number line every value of $h$ that makes the formula true.

canonical_solution.text_md: Put the two given numbers into $I=\dfrac{bh^2}{12}$, so that $h$ is the only letter left.
Do the same to both sides to undo what is joined to $h^2$: multiply by 12, then divide by the number that multiplies $h^2$, until $h^2$ stands alone and equals a positive number.
Ask which numbers square to that value. Taking the square root of both sides gives two answers, the positive root and its negative, because a negative number squared is also positive.
Tap the positive root on the number line, then tap the negative root: two points the same distance from 0, one on each side.

questions.stem: In the formula $I=\dfrac{1}{2}M\left(a^2+b^2\right)$, $a=4$, $M=8$ and $I=320$. Mark on the number line every value of $b$ that makes the formula true.

canonical_solution.text_md: Put the three given numbers into $I=\dfrac{1}{2}M\left(a^2+b^2\right)$, so that $b$ is the only letter left.
Undo what multiplies the bracket by doing the same to both sides: multiply by 2, then divide by $M$.
Subtract the number $a^2$ from both sides so that $b^2$ stands alone and equals a positive number.
Take the square root of both sides: the positive root and its negative both square to this number, so $b$ has two values.
Tap both values on the number line, one on each side of 0.

questions.stem: Solve $-4 < 2x - 2 \le 8$ for $x$, where $x$ is a real number. Then mark the solution on the number line: choose where the solution starts and where it ends, and make each end hollow if that number is not included, or filled if it is.

pending_review.why: It is listed for interval mode, so it can fire. The construction that fires it is any pair of endpoints other than -1 and 5, for example (-4, 8] or (-2, 4] from the middle-only slip. But the predicate is a parameter-free catch-all for 'wrong endpoints' and cannot tell that slip from a sign slip, such as subtracting 2 and getting (-3, 3], from not dividing the ends, or from other arithmetic errors. A student with an unrelated slip would be told she changed only the middle, so it is not a safe diagnosis.

canonical_solution.text_md: Whatever you do to one part of a double inequality you must do to all three parts, so that both inequalities stay true together.
Add 2 to all three parts: $-4 < 2x - 2 \le 8$ becomes $-2 < 2x \le 10$.
Divide all three parts by $2$: $-2 < 2x \le 10$ becomes $-1 < x \le 5$. Dividing by a positive number leaves both signs as they are.
So the solution is every real $x$ in $-1 < x \le 5$: it starts at $-1$ and ends at $5$.
The sign beside $-1$ is $<$, so $-1$ is not included: hollow circle. The sign beside $5$ is $\le$, so $5$ is included: filled circle.

questions.stem: Solve $-3 \le 3x + 6 < 12$ for $x$, where $x$ is a real number. Then mark the solution on the number line: choose where the solution starts and where it ends, and make each end hollow if that number is not included, or filled if it is.

pending_review.why: It can fire in interval mode. It fires on any endpoints other than -3 and 2, for example [-1, 4) from the middle-only slip with a full divide. It would fire identically for other errors: adding 6 instead of subtracting gives -3 <= x < 6 (that is, [-3, 6)), dividing only some parts, or arithmetic slips. It cannot isolate operate-on-middle-only, so the specific refutation would often be served for a mistake the student did not make.

canonical_solution.text_md: Whatever you do to one part of a double inequality you must do to all three parts, so that both inequalities stay true together.
Subtract 6 from all three parts: $-3 \le 3x + 6 < 12$ becomes $-9 \le 3x < 6$.
Divide all three parts by $3$: $-9 \le 3x < 6$ becomes $-3 \le x < 2$. Dividing by a positive number leaves both signs as they are.
So the solution is every real $x$ in $-3 \le x < 2$: it starts at $-3$ and ends at $2$.
The sign beside $-3$ is $\le$, so $-3$ is included: filled circle. The sign beside $2$ is $<$, so $2$ is not included: hollow circle.

questions.stem: Solve $-2 \le 2x - 6 \le 4$ for $x$, where $x$ is a real number. Then mark the solution on the number line: choose where the solution starts and where it ends, and make each end hollow if that number is not included, or filled if it is.

pending_review.why: It can fire in interval mode. It fires on any endpoints other than 2 and 5, for example [-1, 2] from the middle-only slip with a full divide. But that is the same firing as for a sign slip (subtracting 6 gives -4 <= x <= -1), for forgetting to divide, or for arithmetic slips. The predicate has no signature specific to leaving the outer numbers unchanged, so it would mostly fire for other reasons and cannot be attributed to this misconception.

canonical_solution.text_md: Whatever you do to one part of a double inequality you must do to all three parts, so that both inequalities stay true together.
Add 6 to all three parts: $-2 \le 2x - 6 \le 4$ becomes $4 \le 2x \le 10$.
Divide all three parts by $2$: $4 \le 2x \le 10$ becomes $2 \le x \le 5$. Dividing by a positive number leaves both signs as they are.
So the solution is every real $x$ in $2 \le x \le 5$: it starts at $2$ and ends at $5$.
Both signs are $\le$, so both $2$ and $5$ are included: both circles are filled.

questions.stem: Solve $0 < 4x - 4 < 16$ for $x$, where $x$ is a real number. Then mark the solution on the number line: choose where the solution starts and where it ends, and make each end hollow if that number is not included, or filled if it is.

pending_review.why: It can fire in interval mode. It fires on any endpoints other than 1 and 5, for example (0, 4) from the middle-only slip with a full divide. But it also fires for sign slips (subtracting 4 gives -1 < x < 3, that is (-1, 3)), for dividing only the middle, or for arithmetic slips. It is a generic wrong-endpoints test, so it cannot confirm that the student left the outer numbers unchanged, and the diagnosis could be served to a student who did not make that mistake.

canonical_solution.text_md: Whatever you do to one part of a double inequality you must do to all three parts, so that both inequalities stay true together.
Add 4 to all three parts: $0 < 4x - 4 < 16$ becomes $4 < 4x < 20$.
Divide all three parts by $4$: $4 < 4x < 20$ becomes $1 < x < 5$. Dividing by a positive number leaves both signs as they are.
So the solution is every real $x$ in $1 < x < 5$: it starts at $1$ and ends at $5$.
Both signs are $<$, so neither $1$ nor $5$ is included: both circles are hollow.

questions.stem: Solve $-3 < x - 2 \le 4$ for $x$, where $x$ is a real number. Then mark the solution on the number line: choose where the solution starts and where it ends, and make each end hollow if that number is not included, or filled if it is.

canonical_solution.text_md: A double inequality has three parts: the left end, the middle and the right end. Whatever you do to one part you must do to all three, so that both inequalities stay true together.
Add 2 to all three parts: $-3 < x - 2 \le 4$ becomes $-1 < x \le 6$.
So the solution is every real $x$ in $-1 < x \le 6$: it starts at $-1$ and ends at $6$.
The sign beside $-1$ is $<$, so $-1$ is not included: hollow circle. The sign beside $6$ is $\le$, so $6$ is included: filled circle.

misconceptions.label: Throws away a negative solution without checking
misconceptions.description: The student drops the negative solution every time, as a habit, even when the problem puts no sign condition on the unknown.

misconceptions.label: Keeps a solution the problem rules out
misconceptions.description: The student factorises correctly and finds both solutions of the equation, then gives both (or the wrong one) as the answer without checking each against the conditions the problem states about the unknown.

misconceptions.label: Writes only the positive root
misconceptions.description: After isolating the squared variable, the student takes the square root of both sides but writes only the positive value, so one of the two answers is lost.

misconceptions.label: Changing only the middle part of a double inequality
misconceptions.description: The student removes the number added to or taken from the middle part of a double inequality but leaves the numbers at the two ends unchanged.
